clinicalScope: Normal adult kidney anatomy and related clinical correlations for Year‑4 medical students working in East African low‑resource hospitals
title: Kidney Anatomy and Clinical Correlations
subject: Anatomy
summary: The kidneys are bean‑shaped retroperitoneal organs that filter blood, regulate fluid balance and produce hormones. Understanding their position, blood supply and relations helps you interpret symptoms, plan investigations and avoid surgical pitfalls.

b: Bean‑shaped, about 11 cm long, 6 cm wide, 3 cm thick
Right kidney usually 1–2 cm lower because of the liver
Located between the peritoneum (anterior) and psoas major muscle (posterior)
Divided into cortex, medulla, and renal pelvis

sections.p: Kidneys develop from intermediate mesoderm through three successive stages: pronephros, mesonephros and metanephros; the metanephric blastema and ureteric bud interact to form nephrons and collecting system.
b: Metanephros appears at week 5 and becomes functional by week 9
Ureteric bud gives rise to collecting ducts, calyces, pelvis and ureter
Metanephric mesenchyme forms glomeruli, proximal/distal tubules, loops of Henle
Ascent from pelvic region to lumbar position explains occasional ectopic kidneys

sections.p: Each kidney is covered by perirenal fat and the renal fascia (Gerota’s fascia). Anteriorly it contacts the duodenum (right) or spleen (left); posteriorly it rests on psoas major, quadratus lumborum and transversus abdominis.
b: Anterior relations: liver (right), spleen and stomach (left)
Posterior relations: psoas major, quadratus lumborum, 12th rib
Superior pole: adrenal gland separated by a thin connective septum
Inferior pole: renal vessels cross the aortic bifurcation (right) or iliac vessels (left)

sections.p: Renal arteries arise from the abdominal aorta just below the origin of the superior mesenteric artery; they branch segmentally to supply the cortex and medulla. Venous drainage follows the renal veins into the inferior vena cava.
b: Single main renal artery (often multiple segmental branches)
Segmental arteries are end‑arteries – no collateral flow
Renal vein drains directly into IVC (right) or via left renal vein to IVC
Accessory renal arteries occur in ~30 % of individuals, important for surgery

sections.p: Sympathetic fibers from T10–L2 travel with the renal arteries; parasympathetic input is minimal. Lymph drains to para‑aortic (lumbar) nodes.
b: Sympathetic stimulation causes renal vasoconstriction and renin release
Pain from renal capsule is referred to T10–L1 dermatomes (flank)
Lymphatics follow arterial branches to lumbar (para‑aortic) nodes
No direct lymphatic drainage to inguinal nodes – useful in staging cancers

sections.p: The cortex contains glomeruli, proximal and distal tubules, and part of the loop of Henle; the medulla is organized into renal pyramids with loops of Henle and collecting ducts.
b: Glomerulus: tuft of capillaries within Bowman's capsule – filtration unit
Proximal tubule: brush border, reabsorbs 65 % of filtered Na⁺ and water
Loop of Henle: descending limb permeable to water, ascending limb to Na⁺/K⁺
Collecting duct: regulated by antidiuretic hormone (ADH) for water reabsorption

sections.p: Kidneys maintain fluid‑electrolyte balance, acid‑base homeostasis, excrete waste, and produce erythropoietin, renin and active vitamin D.
b: Glomerular filtration rate (GFR) ≈ 125 mL/min/1.73 m² in healthy adult
Tubular reabsorption recovers ~180 L of filtrate daily
Renin‑angiotensin‑aldosterone system (RAAS) controls blood pressure
Erythropoietin stimulates red‑cell production; deficiency causes anemia

sections.p: Knowledge of renal anatomy guides bedside assessment, imaging interpretation and procedural safety (e.g., percutaneous nephrostomy, renal biopsy).
b: Flank pain radiating to the groin suggests ureteric obstruction
Palpable mass above the 12th rib may be an enlarged kidney or tumor
Understanding segmental arteries prevents inadvertent ischemia during nephrectomy
Renal capsule stretch produces dull, constant flank pain

sections.p: Trauma, obstructive uropathy and vascular lesions are the most frequent renal problems encountered in low‑resource settings.
b: Blunt abdominal trauma → renal laceration; look for gross hematuria
Ureteric stones (often calcium oxalate) cause colicky flank pain and hematuria
Renal artery thrombosis → sudden loss of function, flank pain, hypertension
Nephroptosis (floating kidney) may mimic an abdominal mass in upright patients

sections.p: Physical exam combined with ultrasound (first‑line) and, when available, CT scan provides essential diagnostic information.

t.b: Detects flank tenderness, palpable kidney, shifting dullness for ascites; tenderness suggests renal pathology
Answers: Is there hydronephrosis or a solid mass? – Dilated pelvis >5 mm indicates obstruction
Answers: Is renal function impaired? – eGFR <60 mL/min/1.73 m² defines CKD stage 3
Answers: What is stone size/composition? – Stones >5 mm often need intervention

sections.p: Anatomical variants are common and may affect clinical decision‑making.
b: Accessory renal arteries – increase risk of intra‑operative bleeding
Horseshoe kidney – fused lower poles, may cause ureteric obstruction
Pelvic kidney – ectopic, prone to infection and calculi
Duplication of collecting system – can cause recurrent UTIs

sections.p: A systematic bedside strategy ensures you capture key anatomical clues and avoid missing life‑threatening signs.
b: Ask about flank pain, hematuria, urinary frequency, recent trauma or surgery
Inspect for abdominal distension, visible masses, scars from prior surgery
Palpate kidneys 2 cm above the iliac crest at the mid‑axillary line; note tenderness or a palpable organ
Percuss for flank dullness (renal capsule) versus tympany (bowel)
Auscultate for abdominal bruits that may indicate renal artery stenosis

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe flank pain with anuria
Rapid rise in serum creatinine (>0.3 mg/dL in 48 h)
Signs of sepsis with suspected renal infection

faq.q: Why is the right kidney lower than the left?
faq.a: The liver occupies the right upper quadrant, pushing the right kidney down by about 1–2 cm.

faq.q: What does a “segmental artery” mean for surgery?
faq.a: Each segmental artery supplies a distinct renal zone without collateral flow; ligating one causes infarction of that zone.

faq.q: Can a kidney be felt in a healthy adult?
faq.a: Usually not; a palpable kidney suggests enlargement, mass, or ectopia and warrants imaging.

exam: A 35‑year‑old farmer presents with sudden left flank pain after a fall; urine is grossly red. What is your immediate bedside assessment and why? — Check for flank tenderness, assess hemodynamics, obtain bedside ultrasound to look for renal laceration or perinephric hematoma; urgent surgical consult if expanding hematoma.

Explain how the segmental arterial pattern influences the choice of clamping during a partial nephrectomy. — Each segmental artery is end‑arterial; selective clamping preserves uninvolved renal tissue and reduces postoperative loss of GFR.

A patient has a palpable mass 3 cm above the left iliac crest. How does renal anatomy help you differentiate a renal mass from an enlarged spleen? — The left kidney lies higher than the spleen; a mass in the flank with a smooth, firm capsule suggests renal origin, whereas spleen is more mobile and located under the left costal margin.

Why is bedside ultrasound preferred over CT for initial assessment of suspected hydronephrosis in a low‑resource setting? — Ultrasound is portable, radiation‑free, inexpensive, and can detect pelvic dilation >5 mm, guiding urgent decompression.

Describe the clinical significance of an accessory renal artery encountered during a donor nephrectomy. — It must be preserved or re‑anastomosed; failure can cause segmental infarction and postoperative hypertension.

A child presents with recurrent UTIs; ultrasound shows duplicated collecting system. What anatomical feature explains the infections? — The upper pole ureter may have an ectopic insertion (ureterocele) causing stasis and infection.
How does the renal capsule contribute to the pain pattern of a renal colic? — Stretch of the capsule produces dull, constant flank pain, while ureteric spasm adds colicky radiation to the groin.

What are the key differences in physical examination between a renal mass and a hepatic mass? — Renal mass is located in the flank, does not shift with respiration; hepatic mass moves with respiration and is more superior.

In a patient with uncontrolled hypertension, what renal anatomical finding would you suspect and why? — Renal artery stenosis (often at the ostium) reduces perfusion, activates RAAS, raising blood pressure.

A patient cannot lie supine due to severe flank pain; what does this suggest about the underlying anatomy? — Pain from renal capsule irritation is worsened by pressure on the kidney; suggests renal inflammation or obstruction.
